claims.text: The creep resistance of the FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating is primarily controlled by the density and stability of FCC/BCC interphase boundaries.
The as-deposited coating contains interconnected FCC and BCC phases.
The as-deposited coating has abundant, coherent, nanoscale FCC/BCC interphase boundaries.
FCC/BCC interphase boundaries are strong obstacles to dislocation motion and impede slip transfer.
FCC/BCC interphase boundaries restrict lattice diffusion through the coating.
Lattice diffusion can control creep deformation under sustained high-temperature loading.
Dislocation-mediated deformation is active in a dual-phase FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy.
The interphase boundaries enhance work hardening in the as-deposited coating.
Partial homogenization can reduce FCC/BCC interphase-boundary density and phase contrast without changing the overall alloy chemistry.
Reducing interphase-boundary density will make dislocation motion easier.
Reducing interphase-boundary density will increase the steady-state creep rate.
Reducing interphase-boundary density will increase accumulated plastic strain.
Reducing interphase-boundary density will lower the effective creep stress exponent.
A coating retaining a high density of FCC/BCC interfaces will accumulate less creep strain than a heat-treated coating under identical loading.
The proposed mechanism should operate at moderate-to-high temperatures and sustained stresses where lattice diffusion and dislocation motion are both active.
Outside the proposed temperature or stress regime, oxidation or brittle fracture may obscure the contribution of interphase boundaries.
Failure of a reduced-boundary-density sample to show a statistically significant increase in creep rate or total creep strain relative to the as-deposited control would falsify the hypothesis.
